newsitem.title: IRAQ: Kurd group backed by Baghdad take key Iraqi city.
newsitem.headline: Kurd group backed by Baghdad take key Iraqi city.

text.p: An Iraqi Kurdish militia allied to Baghdad captured the main stronghold of its Kurdish rival on Monday in a lightning drive through northern Iraq that raised fears of a refugee crisis.

The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) of Massoud Barzani said its forces had met little resistance from Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) fighters as they swept into the city of Sulaimaniya near the border with Iran.
"The battle for Sulaimaniya is over. Massoud Barzani fighters have entered the city without fighting," a U.N. official told Reuters in Baghdad by telephone from Arbil.
The city, with a population of around a million, is the biggest Kurdish urban centre in Iraq and had long been the headquarters of Jalal Talabani's PUK.
It lies 50 km (30 miles) from Iran which appealed for help to deal with a possible exodus of civilians fleeing the clashes.

State-run Tehran radio quoted Ahmad Hosseini, Tehran's top official in charge of refugees, as saying Iran would make it possible for countries and international organisations to provide relief in camps located in border areas.
Hosseini said 500,000 Kurds had been made homeless or were on the run because of the inter-Kurdish fighting and needed food, clothing and heating equipment, the radio said.
"If world bodies send the needed aid in time we will be able to avoid a human tragedy," Hosseini said.
More than a million Iraqis, most of them Kurds, fled to Iran when Baghdad crushed Kurdish and Shi'ite Moslem uprisings after Iraq's defeat in the 1991 Gulf War.
Most of the Kurds later returned to northern Iraq which has been split into rival Kurdish zones since 1994.
The KDP said Sulaimaniya residents had welcomed its forces.
"They were welcomed by the local population with flowers," leading KDP commander Dr Ross Nouri Shawis told reporters at Dukan, 70 km (45 miles) from the city.
U.N. sources in Baghdad said they could not give a figure on casualties or the number of people displaced in the factional fighting.
The KDP seized the international spotlight on August 31 when, aided by Iraqi troops, it took the Kurdish capital Arbil from the PUK.

The United States retaliated against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein by firing cruise missiles on southern Iraq and extending a southern no-fly zone to the outskirts of Baghdad. But U.S. officials have since said the latest fighting appeared to be a Kurdish civil war without direct Iraqi involvement.
PUK appeals to the United States for help this week have apparently fallen on deaf ears.
Barzani's group says it took Sulaimaniya and nearby towns without the help of the Iraqi government.
There was no sign of Iraqi government troops or weapons as the KDP took the strategic Dukan Dam on its push to Sulaimaniya earlier on Monday.
Veteran warlord Barzani defended his military cooperation with Saddam, his erstwhile arch-foe.

"We don't have anything to apologise for. We did it openly, not secretly," he told reporters at Dukan. His group sent a message of support to Saddam from Sulaimaniya, said Iraqi television, monitored by the BBC.
"With hearts full of faith, we pray to almighty God to keep you as an asset for this homeland and a lofty symbol for all dignified Iraqis," the television quoted the message as saying.
There was no immediate comment on the fall of Sulaimaniya from the PUK and U.N. officials said they did not know the fate of its leader Talabani.

Analysts said it was likely that PUK fighters would regroup in Iran. Talabani has openly warned the KDP and the West that without outside help he would be forced to turn to Tehran for help. The KDP has justified its new alliance with Iraq by accusing the PUK of siding with Iran.
